books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Amnesty Act of May 22, 1872, ch. 193, 17 Stat. 142
Rutherford B. Hayes, Inaugural Address, March 5, 1877

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources and real data (see each document’s sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which Reconstruction had failed by 1877.

documents.title: Amnesty Act restores former Confederates to office
documents.source: Amnesty Act of May 22, 1872, ch. 193, 17 Stat. 142. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Congress, voting by the two-thirds the Fourteenth Amendment required, lifting the officeholding ban on former Confederates.
documents.text: “That all political disabilities imposed by the third section of the fourteenth article of amendments of the Constitution of the United States are hereby removed from all persons whomsoever, except Senators and Representatives of the thirty-sixth and thirty-seventh Congresses, officers in the judicial, military, and naval service of the United States, heads of departments, and foreign ministers of the United States.”

documents.title: The Fifteenth Amendment: the vote in the Constitution
documents.source: Fifteenth Amendment to the Constitution, ratified February 3, 1870. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The amendment as ratified, putting Black men’s suffrage in the Constitution.
documents.text: “Section 1. The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude. Section 2. The Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation.”

documents.title: Nast: “The Lost Cause, Worse than Slavery”
documents.source: Thomas Nast, “The Union as It Was — The Lost Cause, Worse than Slavery,” Harper’s Weekly, October 24, 1874 (Library of Congress, LCCN2001696840). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Thomas Nast, a pro-Reconstruction Northern cartoonist, drawing for the readers of Harper’s Weekly.
documents.text: A man marked “White League,” a rifle on his back, shakes hands with a hooded Klansman marked “K.K.” over a shield. Above them an eagle carries the words “The Union as It Was” and “This Is a White Man’s Government.” Inside the shield, a Black mother and father crouch over their baby in grief, while behind them a freedman hangs from a tree and a schoolhouse burns. A child’s primer lies dropped on the ground.

documents.title: House seats swing to the Democrats
documents.source: Office of the House Historian, “Majority Changes in the House of Representatives, 1856 to Present” (history.house.gov).
documents.sourcing: The House Historian’s count of seats after the 1872 and 1874 elections (initial division of seats).

documents.title: Cruikshank: the amendment binds states, not private men
documents.source: United States v. Cruikshank, 92 U.S. 542 (1876), majority opinion of Chief Justice Morrison Waite. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Chief Justice Waite, overturning the federal convictions from the Colfax Massacre prosecutions.
documents.text: “The fourteenth amendment prohibits a State from depriving any person of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law; but this adds nothing to the rights of one citizen as against another. . . . The fourteenth amendment prohibits a State from denying to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws; but this provision does not, any more than the one which precedes it, and which we have just considered, add any thing to the rights which one citizen has under the Constitution against another.”

documents.title: The disputed presidential election
documents.source: Rutherford B. Hayes Presidential Library & Museums, “Frequently Asked Questions on the 1876 Election.”
documents.sourcing: The Hayes Presidential Library’s figures for the disputed election of 1876.
documents.text:
| 1876 presidential election | Samuel J. Tilden (Democrat) | Rutherford B. Hayes (Republican) |
| Popular vote | 4,288,546 | 4,034,311 |
| Electoral votes, first count | 184 | 165 |

Twenty electoral votes were disputed: Florida (4), Louisiana (8), South Carolina (7), and one from Oregon. A candidate needed 185 electoral votes to win.

documents.title: Hayes promises local self-government
documents.source: Rutherford B. Hayes, Inaugural Address, March 5, 1877. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: President Hayes, days after the disputed election was settled, telling the country his policy for the South.
documents.text: “The evils which afflict the Southern States can only be removed or remedied by the united and harmonious efforts of both races, actuated by motives of mutual sympathy and regard; and while in duty bound and fully determined to protect the rights of all by every constitutional means at the disposal of my Administration, I am sincerely anxious to use every legitimate influence in favor of honest and efficient local self-government as the true resource of those States for the promotion of the contentment and prosperity of their citizens.”

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which Reconstruction failed by 1877, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as emancipation during the Civil War, the Reconstruction Acts, or the debate over who would control Reconstruction.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about the prompt.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Panic of 1873, the Mississippi Plan of 1875, the Exodus of 1879, sharecropping, or the Civil Rights Cases of 1883.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document’s author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of the claim, showing how the same development pulled in opposite directions, or weighing change against continuity.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Reconstruction had failed to a great extent by 1877, because the federal government gave up the tools that protected Black rights, though the amendments and Black institutions survived its end.
Grouping 1 — the North steps back: the Amnesty Act (Doc 1) restores former Confederates to office, and the 1874 House swing (Doc 4) shows Northern voters turning from Reconstruction to hard times.
Grouping 2 — what survived: the Fifteenth Amendment (Doc 2) put the vote in the Constitution, so the failure was of enforcement, not of every gain.
Grouping 3 — the end on the ground: Nast (Doc 3) shows terror undoing freedom, Cruikshank (Doc 5) leaves that terror unpunished by the federal courts, the disputed election (Doc 6) forces a bargain, and Hayes (Doc 7) announces local self-government as the troops leave.
Outside evidence: the Panic of 1873; the Mississippi Plan of 1875; the Slaughter-House Cases (1873); United States v. Reese (1876); the Exodus of 1879.
Complexity: the same five years that ended federal enforcement left the amendments in the Constitution and Black churches and schools standing, so the failure was of enforcement, not of every gain.
